title: 开发者现可应用 EVE: Frontier 中使用的高端环境光遮蔽技术
content:
Devs can now use EVE: Frontier's high-end lighting technique
Programming
Art
News
Devs can now utilize the high-end ambient occlusion technique seen in EVE: Frontier
CORTAO, a personal programming project by Fenris Creations developer Daniel Isheden, is being used for EVE: Frontier, and maybe your next game.
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
November 23, 2026
schedule
2 Min Read
expand_content
Image via Fenris Creations
Technically-minded developers obsessed with high-quality real-time global illumination have a new resource to tap into this month, thanks to the hard work of developer Daniel Isheden. Isheden, who works at EVE developer Fenris Creations, has released assets for CORTAO, which stands for "Circular Occluder Ray-Traced Ambient Occlusion," as an open-source repository
that you can access here
.
CORTAO, which is a physically based real-time screen space ambient occlusion (SSAO) technique, isn't just a personal pet project for Isheden. His employer has also adopted the technology to be used in
EVE Online
spinoff
EVE: Frontier
, and also
publicly shared its implementation of CORTAO
, which is streamlined to work with the studio's proprietary game engine. This all comes after what Isheden described in an interview with GameDeveloper.com as "over two years of work."
Fenris' support for Isheden's personal release of CORTAO is a rare sight in the video game industry. Many employers consider the development of such techniques to be property of the company, and are often considered a trade secret. This release helps developers working in high-fidelity 3D graphics solve challenging problems concerning global illumination in games, particularly for lower-end devices, which Isheden says CORTAO is able to accommodate.

Existing versions of these techniques are "rarely perfect," Isheden said, and often lack the resolution or accuracy to depict "small-scale details" that make a scene feel "grounded and connected," SSAO techniques are used to close the gap. CORTAO builds on previously techniques in order to compute ambient occlusion to "a higher level of accuracy," adding visual contrast and grounding objects properly. Because this technique "converges faster," it requires less GPU time to work effectively, hence the expanded support for lower-end hardware.
Isheden began developing this technique to better solve what he called "common visual issues in 3D scenes with high-depth complexity," particularly those with detailed vegetation and foliage. The use of screen space raytracing apparently proved to be "extremely flexible," and also a good fit for the ominous celestial landscapes of
EVE: Frontier
. "Its high accuracy and ability to handle a larger occlusion radius than existing techniques made it a great fit for the vast, changing space scenes of a dynamic, player-generated universe," he explained.
That means while developers looking to get as close as possible to the visual realism of a game like
Grand Theft Auto VI
will have a new tool in their toolkit, the technique can also help those looking to what Isheden described as "stylized, non-realistic visuals" as well.
